views.label: No phase kept
views.note: A Fourier transform of n real samples gives n complex numbers, half of them mirrors. Here n samples give n numbers.

views.label: The half sample
views.note: Setting the samples between the ends of the cosine, not on them, makes the signal even at both ends with no step.

views.label: Gathered at the front
views.note: A slow curve becomes a few large numbers and a long tail of nearly nothing, and the tail can be thrown away.

views.label: And back again
views.note: The weights make the two directions mirrors, thus taking one and then the other gives back what went in.

boundaries.label: cost grows with the square of the size

cards.title: What it works out
items: X[k] = weight * sum over n of x[n] * cos(pi*k*(n+0.5)/size)
n real samples become n real numbers, and no phase is kept
A Fourier transform would give 2n numbers, half of them mirrors

cards.title: How the library gets there
items: The weight is sqrt(1/size) for the first output and sqrt(2/size) for the rest
Scaled that way the transform and its undoing are mirrors of each other
The half in (n+0.5) is what makes the signal even at both ends

cards.title: Why it is used everywhere
items: A slow curve of 64 samples needs 4 numbers to hold 0.99 of it, against 20 for the transform
That is why it sits behind the compression of pictures and sound
The cost grows with the square of the size, thus the bound of 1024
